results.key_finding: STN-DBS reduces OFF time, dyskinesia, and levodopa equivalent dose in patients with Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations. Candidacy criteria include: (1) confirmed idiopathic PD with good levodopa response (>30% UPDRS-III improvement), (2) motor fluctuations or dyskinesias not controllable by medication optimization, (3) no significant dementia (MMSE >24 as soft threshold), (4) no major psychiatric disorder, (5) no atypical parkinsonian features.
results.title: Evidence-based efficacy and effectiveness of deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease

results.key_finding: Clinically established PD requires: (a) parkinsonism, (b) absence of absolute exclusion criteria, (c) ≥2 supportive criteria (dramatic levodopa benefit, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, rest tremor, olfactory loss, or cardiac MIBG denervation). Supportive criteria include clear dramatic levodopa responsiveness and levodopa-induced dyskinesia — both present in this context.
results.title: MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease

results.key_finding: PD-MCI (mild cognitive impairment) with executive or memory deficits does not preclude DBS benefit, but PD-dementia (global cognitive decline with functional impairment) is associated with worse outcomes. Formal neuropsychological testing is standard prior to DBS implantation. DRS-2 scores above 130 are generally associated with acceptable DBS outcomes in PD.
results.title: Cognitive screening before deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease

results.key_finding: Motor fluctuations are reliably quantified with the UPDRS Part IV. Wearing-off is defined as predictable re-emergence of parkinsonian features before the next scheduled dose. In patients with >3 hours of daily OFF time despite optimized pharmacotherapy, advanced therapy (DBS or infusion) is indicated.
results.title: Levodopa equivalent dose calculation and wearing-off assessment in advanced Parkinson's disease

alternatives: If antiemetic needed peri-operatively: ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) is the appropriate choice — no dopamine receptor blockade
If antipsychotic needed post-operatively or for psychosis in PD: quetiapine (lowest D2 blockade) or pimavanserin (5-HT2A inverse agonist, no D2 blockade) are preferred agents
Lorazepam alternatives for anxiety/insomnia in PD: low-dose melatonin for sleep-onset; clonazepam 0.5 mg for RBD if polysomnography-confirmed
contraindications: Meperidine (Demerol) is absolutely contraindicated in patients on rasagiline or any MAO-B inhibitor due to risk of serotonin syndrome.

Typical antipsychotics and most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) are contraindicated in parkinsonism — they will worsen PD motor symptoms by blocking dopamine receptors.
Dopamine antagonist antiemetics (prochlorperazine) are contraindicated in PD.
interactions: MAJOR: Rasagiline (MAO-B inhibitor) interacts with multiple serotonergic and sympathomimetic drugs. Any planned peri-operative use of meperidine, tramadol, or certain anesthetics (e.g., sympathomimetics) must be communicated to the anesthesia team before DBS surgery.

MODERATE: Lorazepam (benzodiazepine) combined with pramipexole (dopamine agonist) increases sedation risk. Benzodiazepine use can also impair postoperative cognitive recovery and augment confusion in the peri-operative period.
MINOR: Ferrous sulfate reduces levodopa absorption when co-administered. Administer ferrous sulfate at least 2 hours apart from levodopa doses.

CAUTION: Amantadine has anticholinergic properties and may contribute to cognitive side effects; this is particularly relevant in patients with borderline cognitive scores undergoing DBS candidacy evaluation.
output.proposed: Current regimen evaluation for DBS candidacy: carbidopa-levodopa, pramipexole, rasagiline, amantadine, lorazepam
warnings: Rasagiline must be stopped at least 14 days before any surgical procedure requiring general anesthesia that involves sympathomimetic agents or meperidine-based analgesia.
Pramipexole may cause impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating); screen at each visit.
Lorazepam use should be minimized pre- and post-operatively if DBS surgery proceeds.
Amantadine's cognitive and anticholinergic burden should be reassessed against DRS-2 score in this patient.
Iron supplementation must be timed away from levodopa doses to prevent reduced levodopa bioavailability.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe dopamine antagonist antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, haloperidol) — these will acutely worsen PD motor symptoms.

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) if psychosis arises; restrict to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin.
Do not co-administer meperidine or tramadol with rasagiline — risk of serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis.
Do not administer ferrous sulfate within 2 hours of levodopa doses.
Do not diagnose PD-dementia (a relative contraindication to DBS) without formal full neuropsychological testing in the ON state; MoCA alone is insufficient to determine DBS ineligibility.
required_recommendations: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: confirm clinically established PD (bradykinesia plus rest tremor and rigidity, dramatic levodopa response, levodopa-induced dyskinesia as supportive criteria, no absolute exclusion features, no red flags).

Recognize that coexisting essential tremor (postural/action tremor predating PD onset by >8 years, family history in mother) does not invalidate the PD diagnosis — rest tremor, left-predominant bradykinesia, and rigidity independently satisfy MDS criteria.

Assess DBS candidacy: confirm levodopa responsiveness (>30% UPDRS-III improvement), characterize OFF time burden (>3 h/day), and differentiate PD-MCI from PD-dementia via formal neuropsychological battery.
Flag ferrous sulfate as a pharmacokinetic confounder: iron chelates levodopa and reduces bioavailability when co-administered; separate doses by at least 2 hours to improve ON period quality.
Communicate rasagiline (MAO-B inhibitor) to the surgical and anesthesia teams: meperidine and certain sympathomimetic anesthetic agents are absolutely contraindicated peri-operatively.

Screen for and document REM sleep behavior disorder (husband-confirmed dream enactment); if confirmed by polysomnography, this provides additional synucleinopathy biomarker evidence supporting idiopathic PD diagnosis.
Review lorazepam use: benzodiazepine use increases peri-operative cognitive risk and sedation; minimize or discontinue before DBS surgery if possible.

No syncope, arrhythmia, or cardiac concern requiring rhythm monitoring.
Amyloid PET is not indicated in PD evaluation; DaTscan is the relevant presynaptic dopaminergic imaging test for this condition.

key_clinical_evidence: Idiopathic PD is confirmed by 9-year asymmetric left-predominant parkinsonism with documented dramatic levodopa response and levodopa-induced dyskinesia — two MDS 2015 supportive criteria satisfied; no red flags or absolute exclusion criteria.
Coexisting essential tremor does not invalidate the PD diagnosis; the key is identifying which tremor component is which (rest vs. postural/action) and recognizing dual pathology.
Ferrous sulfate co-administration with levodopa is a pharmacokinetic red herring: it is a correctable cause of suboptimal levodopa delivery that can masquerade as disease progression or wearing-off.

Formal neuropsychological testing (DRS-2, HVLT-R, fluency) is load-bearing for DBS candidacy: the patient's multi-domain PD-MCI pattern does not preclude DBS but requires explicit documentation; the cognitive status cannot be adjudicated from MoCA alone.
Rasagiline peri-operative safety is a non-obvious but clinically critical interaction: this MAO-B inhibitor mandates anesthesia team communication before surgery.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Parkinson's disease is a clinical diagnosis under the MDS criteria; laboratory testing excludes a mimic when one is suspected.
July 2026 review applied: PD remains a clinical diagnosis; no fixed routine laboratory panel, EEG, ECG, formal autonomic or tilt-table testing is part of the PD diagnostic pathway.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Layla Haddad is a 58-year-old right-handed Arab-American woman with a 9-year history of Parkinson's disease who presents to the movement disorders clinic for evaluation of advanced therapy candidacy, specifically deep brain stimulation. She is accompanied by her husband and adult daughter.

Ms. Haddad was diagnosed at age 49 with left-arm predominant rest tremor and bradykinesia by a neurologist in her home country before immigrating to the United States four years ago. Initial levodopa response was described as dramatic. Over the past three years, she has developed significant motor fluctuations characterized by predictable wearing-off starting approximately 3.5–4 hours after each dose, with morning OFF periods lasting 1.5 to 2 hours until her first dose takes effect. Her husband describes the morning OFF state vividly: she is rigid, tremulous, unable to button her clothes or rise from bed unassisted, speaks very quietly, and becomes visibly distressed. During ON periods she functions substantially better, though she has developed peak-dose dyskinesias — bilateral arm and trunk writhing movements — that begin approximately 60–90 minutes after each levodopa dose and persist for 30–60 minutes. These dyskinesias are embarrassing and are limiting her social functioning and ability to attend her daughter's school events.

Currently she takes carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg four times daily, with pramipexole 1.5 mg three times daily added 18 months ago to reduce inter-dose wearing-off, rasagiline 1 mg once daily (started 2 years ago), and amantadine 100 mg twice daily for dyskinesia (started 9 months ago). Despite this regimen, she still experiences 3–4 hours of OFF time daily and peak-dose dyskinesias with nearly every dose.

A confounding issue is a pre-existing bilateral postural/action tremor that dates to her early 40s, before any parkinsonian features appeared, and is present in her mother. This tremor does not respond to levodopa but is separate from the rest tremor of her PD. Her previous neurologist documented this as 'essential tremor coexisting with PD,' though some clinicians have questioned whether she has essential tremor at all or whether the postural tremor is part of PD.

Cognitive concerns: family members note she is slower to process information and occasionally has word-finding difficulty. She scored 25/30 on MoCA in the ON state. The movement disorders team is concerned about whether her cognitive status meets criteria for DBS candidacy (mild cognitive impairment requires careful characterization to assess whether she has PD-MCI, which may be acceptable, versus PD-dementia, which is a relative contraindication).

She has no history of significant psychiatric illness apart from anxiety, treated with as-needed lorazepam. She has no hallucinations. She denies significant falls in the past 6 months, though her husband reports 2 falls in the past 4 months, one resulting in a bruised hip. Review of systems is notable for constipation, anosmia (~5 years), and occasional lightheadedness on standing (no syncope).

Medications: she is on ferrous sulfate for iron-deficiency anemia. She was previously prescribed ondansetron for nausea and has taken it sporadically. Lorazepam is used intermittently at night.

The movement disorders team is evaluating her for STN-DBS candidacy and wishes to confirm: (1) exclusion of atypical parkinsonism, (2) adequate levodopa responsiveness, (3) cognitive screen sufficient for DBS, (4) medication safety review including lorazepam and rasagiline interactions with future peri-operative and post-operative regimens.

neurological_exam.additional: Seborrheic dermatitis on forehead and nasolabial folds. Constipation reported (2–3 movements per week). Husband notes she has acted out vivid dreams on at least three occasions over the past year — kicking and vocalizing during sleep. Patient reports anosmia of approximately 5 years duration, which preceded worsening of motor fluctuations. No autonomic syncope; reports mild dizziness on standing occasionally but no orthostatic falls.

No supranuclear vertical gaze palsy. Facial hypomimia, bilaterally symmetric, severe. Blink rate markedly reduced. Cranial nerves V, VII (motor), IX, X, XI, XII intact. Convergence mildly impaired. No ptosis.

Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 25/30 in the ON state: loses 2 points on delayed recall, 1 on executive/trail-making, 1 on naming, 1 on visuospatial. Patient reports she 'can't concentrate' during OFF periods and that her scores are worse in the morning before first dose. No frank confusion, hallucinations, or delusions. Affect mildly anxious.
neurological_exam.motor: Moderate cogwheel rigidity at bilateral wrists and elbows, more pronounced on the left. Bradykinesia markedly worse on the left: left-hand finger tapping shows rapid amplitude decrement and speed reduction; right hand mildly slowed. Left upper extremity rest tremor 4–5 Hz, pill-rolling, constant during the examination (patient is in a partial OFF state at time of exam). Strength 5/5 throughout. No pronator drift. Left lower extremity mildly stiffer than right. No involuntary choreiform movements observed at time of examination (patient reports peak-dose dyskinesias involve bilateral arm and trunk writhing, typically 1–2 hours after each levodopa dose, lasting 30–60 minutes).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Glabellar reflex positive.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact bilaterally. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes. Proprioception intact at toes.
